findings.summary: DETECTION IS UNBOUNDED-DEPTH BUT ANSWERING IS TAIL-BOUNDED, AND THE ADR CLAIMS OTHERWISE. M4.10b's row states the property first and in the strongest terms: 'A replay must be ANSWERED, not merely detected: M4.10d must return the original offsets, so whatever is recorded has to lead back to them.' What this ADR records is a bare watermark -- Checkpoint.pods becomes podId -> (incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq) (l.58-60) -- and a watermark leads back to nothing. It is a comparison, not a pointer. The Consequences section papers over this with 'Answering costs nothing extra. The delta carrying the triple also carries SegmentCommit.segmentKey and RunCommit.firstOffset ... so whatever detects a replay can answer it from the same object' (l.75-77). But detection and answering do not read the same object and do not have the same reach. Detection is in-memory against the watermark recovered from the checkpoint, and reaches every flushSeq the incarnation ever issued. Answering needs the specific CommitDelta that carried flushSeq=N, and the ADR's very next paragraph explains why that delta is unreachable once a checkpoint has passed it: 'Entries below the newest checkpoint are never GET -- the Hop javadoc says they "are never GET at all"' (l.81-83). Verified in the code: ChainReplay.java:369 starts the LIST at keyFor(hop.from() - 1), so entries below the seeded checkpoint are neither listed nor GET, and Checkpoint (format/src/main/java/binjava/format/Checkpoint.java:42-44) carries only per-stream offsets and Map<String, Long> pods -- nothing maps a flushSeq to a chain slot or to that commit's offsets. So the answerable depth is exactly M4.9's bound, 'the newest checkpoint plus at most K deltas' (ADR-0033), i.e. CheckpointWriter's everyDeltas. THIS IS THE ALTERNATIVE THE ADR ITSELF REJECTS. 'Bound the window to the uncheckpointed tail. Rejected: a replay older than the newest checkpoint would be neither detected nor answered' (l.129-130). The decision half-shares that defect -- such a replay is detected but NOT answered -- and nowhere says so. The rewrite introduced the gap: the superseded draft carried a per-pod segment-key pointer and claimed, correctly for its own mechanism, 'A replay older than the newest checkpoint is answerable through the per-pod pointer'. This draft removes the pointer on size grounds (l.92-93, MAX_KEY_BYTES 1024 per pod -- verified at binstore-backends/src/main/java/binjava/binstore/backend/LocalFsBinStore.java:52) and does not replace the answering mechanism, while keeping the claim that answering is free. Nor is there a cheap replacement lying around: storing the offsets per pod is bounded by (pod, stream) pairs, which the superseded draft rejected against ADR-0033's size argument, and resolving the replay by walking the chain backwards is forbidden by the row ('Resolving a replay by walking the chain backwards is the same fault in GETs'). That is precisely why the tension needed confronting in the Decision rather than eliding in a Consequence.
findings.failure_scenario: The next session picks M4.10d, whose row -- rewritten by this same diff -- instructs it to key on (podId, incarnationId, flushSeq) and answer a replay 'with the ORIGINAL offsets', and reads this ADR's 'Answering costs nothing extra' as licence that no further mechanism is owed. It implements detection against the recovered watermark, which works to unbounded depth, and answering by looking up the flushSeq in the deltas it replayed. It then writes the anchor test the row demands, and that test passes: the test's replay is a recent one, so its delta is still in the uncheckpointed tail. In a deployment with CheckpointWriter's everyDeltas triggering normally, a replay of a commit older than the newest checkpoint is refused -- correctly -- but cannot be answered, because nothing durable maps flushSeq=N to its offsets and the delta that held them is below hop.from() and is never GET. The producer receives a refusal with no offsets for records that ARE durable and DID commit, so it cannot complete its AppendResult and must either fail the append (data the caller was told nothing about) or re-flush the same records under a new flushSeq (the duplicate M4.10 exists to prevent). Discovering this at M4.10d costs a second Checkpoint format change on top of the one M4.10c will just have shipped -- a wire format, the goldens, the fakes and this ADR again, per non-negotiable 8. Cheap to fix here: either state plainly that answering is bounded to the uncheckpointed tail and detection beyond it refuses without offsets (and say what a producer does with that), or decide the durable pointer now, in the ADR whose job is to decide it.

findings.summary: 'A DIFFERENT incarnationId IS A NEW INCARNATION' IS NOT TRUE, AND IT IS THE PREDICATE M4.10d WILL IMPLEMENT. The ADR asserts it flatly at l.46-47: 'A different incarnationId is a new incarnation and is accepted, which is the case the bare pair got wrong.' A different incarnationId is a DIFFERENT incarnation. It may be an older one. The decision deliberately chooses an identifier with no order -- 'no clock, no coordination' (l.38) -- so the sequencer cannot ask whether an arriving incarnationId is newer or older than the one it holds; a UUID admits no such comparison. That is a real price of the choice, it is the direct consequence of the property the ADR is proudest of, and the document never names it. It is load-bearing because the same ADR decides the checkpoint holds exactly ONE slot per pod (l.58-59, podId -> (incarnationId, lastAppliedFlushSeq)). One unordered slot plus 'different => accept and overwrite' means the unbounded-depth guarantee is not merely absent across incarnations, it is destructible WITHIN one: any request bearing a different incarnationId overwrites the slot, and the live incarnation's own subsequent replays are then read against a foreign watermark and accepted. The ADR advertises the window as 'unbounded-depth: a replay of any earlier commit is caught' (l.43-44); it is caught only while no other incarnation of that podId interleaves. AND THE INTERLEAVING CASE IS ALREADY IN THE CORPUS, which is why 'ADR-0031's argument extends unchanged' (l.105) understates it. ADR-0031 analyses two live processes sharing a podId and concludes the damage is bounded because CommitLog's write-once chain arbitrates every slot, so 'No slot is ever double-won and no offset is ever double-assigned (I1, I2)'. That reasoning is about OFFSET ASSIGNMENT and says nothing about idempotency, which did not exist when it was written. Under this decision the two processes hold distinct UUIDs, each overwrites the other's slot on every commit, and a replay from either is accepted as new -- so the property this ADR adds is degraded by exactly the scenario ADR-0031 declared safe. Extending that argument 'unchanged' is the wrong conclusion; what is owed is a sentence saying the idempotency guarantee, unlike I1/I2, does not survive a podId collision. The second reachable shape is the one the ADR claims immunity from. It rejects the lease epoch because it 'stops the moment M5's commit forwarding lands -- so it passes every test M4 can write' (l.20-21), and claims for itself 'nothing that changes meaning when M5 moves the sequencer out of process' (l.38-39). The KEY's meaning does not change; the sufficiency of one slot per pod does. M4 has no seam at which a request can outlive its issuing process -- DefaultIngest.flushLocked issues and awaits under one lock -- so a dead incarnation issues nothing and the single slot is sufficient by construction. M5 introduces a network between producer and sequencer, and a forwarded request that a transport retries can arrive after its issuer is gone and a successor incarnation has committed. The ADR holds its rejected alternative to a standard ('passes every test M4 can write') that it does not check its own choice against on this axis.
findings.failure_scenario: Concretely today, under ADR-0031's own out-of-protocol-but-analysed scenario: processes X and Y share podId 'poda' and mint incarnations Ix and Iy. X commits (Ix, 5); the slot becomes (Ix, 5). Y commits (Iy, 3); the incarnationId differs, so per l.46-47 it is accepted as a new incarnation and the slot becomes (Iy, 3). X's ambiguous commit at flushSeq=5 is now retried -- the very commit-level retry l.113-115 instructs M4.10d to add -- and is tested against (Iy, 3): different incarnation, therefore 'new', therefore ACCEPTED. The segment is committed twice, offsets are assigned twice for records already durable at earlier offsets, and duplicate records reach the index. That is FR-3's harm, produced by the mechanism written to prevent it, in a case the ADR cites as needing no change. The M5 shape is the same arithmetic with a transport retry in place of Y: ingester incarnation I1 forwards (I1, 7), the pod dies, incarnation I2 restarts and commits (I2, 0) so the slot becomes (I2, 0), the transport redelivers (I1, 7), and it is accepted as new. Neither shape is reproducible by any test M4 can write, because M4 has no seam where a request outlives its issuer -- so this lands green, M4.10d lands green, and it surfaces in M5 as duplicate records with no failing test pointing at it. The fix need not change the decision: state in Consequences that incarnationIds are unordered by construction, that one slot per pod therefore gives no cross-incarnation window, and either accept that with its blast radius named or say which later row owns it -- because once M4.10c ships a scalar slot per pod, widening it to remember more than one incarnation is another Checkpoint format change.

findings.summary: The pre-change-checkpoint consequence assumes a version-tolerant Checkpoint reader that does not exist and that the ADR never asks for. l.95-98 says 'A window recovered from a pre-change checkpoint is empty for those pods, and is ACCEPTED rather than refused ... It closes at the first post-upgrade checkpoint.' For a v0 checkpoint to yield an empty window it must first DECODE, and Checkpoint.decode (format/src/main/java/binjava/format/Checkpoint.java:150-152) is a strict equality check -- 'if (version != VERSION) throw new IOException("unsupported checkpoint version: " + version)' -- against VERSION = 0 (line 49). Widening the pods value forces a bump, and with today's decode the recovered outcome is not an empty window but a hard IOException on the recovery path. The ADR's dual-version sentence (l.68-71, citing M3.0's 'SegmentReader accepts BOTH versions') sits under the CommitDelta bullet and is scoped by its own wording to 'Both delta encodings'; the Checkpoint bullet (l.58-60) says nothing about a version bump or about reading v0. M4.10c's row does say 'readers accept both', so this is a gap in the ADR rather than a certainty of defect.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.10c implements the Checkpoint change from the ADR's Which-formats-change section, bumps Checkpoint.VERSION to 1, and regenerates the goldens; the suite is green because every fixture writes and reads v1. On a rolling upgrade the first successor to take over reads a checkpoint its predecessor wrote at v0, decode throws 'unsupported checkpoint version: 0', and recovery fails outright -- an aborted takeover, which is worse than the duplicate-acceptance this paragraph carefully argues is the acceptable degradation. One clause in the Checkpoint bullet stating that decode must accept v0 and materialise an empty per-pod window would make the paragraph deliverable.

findings.summary: 'flushSeq is dense and monotone within an incarnation' is true of ISSUED values and not of APPLIED ones, and the watermark test needs the latter. In DefaultIngest.java:349 the counter is consumed while building the request -- 'sequencer.commit(new CommitRequest(podShortId, flushSeq++, ...))' -- so a commit that THROWS has already spent its flushSeq, and the next flush issues N+1 over a gap at N that was never applied. 'flushSeq <= lastAppliedFlushSeq' therefore refuses values that were never committed and for which there are no original offsets to answer with, which is the ADR's own primary harm (suppressing a real commit) rather than the duplicate it targets. It is latent today for the reason l.110-116 gives -- no retry exists, and the whole-flush retry re-publishes under a new key -- but M4.10d is instructed to add the retry that makes it reachable, so the ADR is the place to say the predicate is sound only while every value at or below the watermark was actually applied. Related and unstated: the update rule at the far end. CheckpointWriter.java:124-128 folds with 'pods.merge(request.podId(), request.flushSeq(), Math::max)' under a comment justifying max -- 'taking the last one seen would walk the idempotency watermark backwards'. With the triple that merge must become incarnation-aware (replace outright when the incarnationId differs, max only within one), because a new incarnation restarts flushSeq at 0 and Math::max would hold the old high-water and refuse every commit the new incarnation makes. The ADR implies it via 'a different incarnationId is accepted' but never says the merge changes, and the existing comment argues for exactly the wrong behaviour at the one site that must change.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.10c implements the Checkpoint widening and updates CheckpointWriter.capture by widening the value while keeping the Math::max fold its comment defends. A pod restarts, its new incarnation commits flushSeq 0, 1, 2, and the fold keeps the predecessor's watermark (say 400) because 400 > 2; M4.10d's predicate then reads flushSeq <= 400 for a pod whose recorded incarnationId no longer matches, and whichever branch is written first decides whether the restarted pod's every commit is suppressed. Nothing in this ADR contradicts the wrong branch, and the CheckpointWriter comment endorses it.
